title: حِكَايَةُ قَمَرِ الزَّمَانِ
source: William Hay Macnaghten, ed., The Alif Laila, or Book of the Thousand Nights and One Night, vol. 1, Calcutta 1839 (“Calcutta II”), printed pp. 817–818 (Night 174, continuing nights-173), transcribed from the 300 ppi scan (archive.org aliflailaorbooko01macn) by the editors' own transcription. The edition prints the prose essentially unpointed: ALL VOCALIZATION (tashkīl) IS EDITORIAL — ours, not the edition's — and the alphabet button strips it back to the bare rasm as Macnaghten prints it, except where a clear misprint has been corrected (each is noted). Romanization is simplified IJMES. Spelling, including the edition’s Middle Arabic forms, is preserved; clear misprints are corrected in the text, and the note on each gives the print’s reading. Obscure or doubtful forms are kept as printed, vocalized by evident sense and flagged in the notes. Read-aloud audio is a Modern Standard Arabic reading of this vocalised text, synthesized by machine, with word-by-word timing generated the same way.
about: Night 174 continues the tale of Qamar al-Zamān. King Shahramān rebukes his son for answering him so before his troops: no one, he says, has yet taught him manners, and such words would be shameful even from a common man. He has the mamluks untie the prince and imprison him in an old tower of the citadel, where a ruined hall with a ruined well in it is swept, furnished with a bed and lit by a lantern and a candle. Alone there, Qamar al-Zamān repents too late, curses marriage and women, and wishes he had obeyed his father. The king, alone with his vizier, blames him for the quarrel and asks what to do now; the vizier advises fifteen days in prison and then the command to marry, which the prince will not refuse, and dawn overtakes Shahrazād. As with every printed edition of the Nights, this one belongs to the late Egyptian recension (ZER) — an eighteenth-century expansion padded out to a literal 1001 nights; no printed edition is a medieval text, and Macnaghten regularised the language here and there, so some Middle Arabic texture is a nineteenth-century retrofit.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا كَانَتِ اللَّيْلَةُ الرَّابِعَةُ وَالسَّبْعُونَ بَعْدَ الْمِائَةِ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā kānati al-laylatu al-rābiʿatu wa-al-sabʿūna baʿda al-miʾati
sentences.l: And when it was the night, the fourth and the seventy after the hundred,
sentences.i: And when it was the hundred and seventy-fourth night,
sentences.n: The formula as before, with al-rābiʿa, “the fourth”, feminine to agree with layla. The units come first and are joined to the tens by wa-, al-rābiʿatu wa-al-sabʿūna, “the fourth and the seventy”, and baʿda al-miʾati, “after the hundred”, adds the hundreds.

sentences.t: قَالَتْ بَلَغَنِي أَيُّهَا الْمَلِكُ السَّعِيدُ أَنَّ الْمَلِكَ شَهْرَمَانَ قَالَ لِوَلَدِهِ قَمَرِ الزَّمَانِ كَيْفَ يَكُونُ هَذَا جَوَابَكَ لِي بَيْنَ عَسَاكِرِي وَجُيُوشِي
sentences.tr: qālat balaghanī ayyuhā al-maliku al-saʿīdu anna al-malika Shahramāna qāla li-waladihi Qamari al-Zamāni kayfa yakūnu hādhā jawābaka lī bayna ʿasākirī wa-juyūshī
sentences.l: She-said: It-has-reached-me, O fortunate king, that the-king Shahramān said to-his-son Qamar al-Zamān: How is this your-answer to-me among my-troops and my-armies?
sentences.i: She said: It has reached me, O fortunate king, that King Shahramān said to his son Qamar al-Zamān, “How can this be your answer to me, in front of my troops and my armies?
sentences.n: Shahrazād takes up the king's words where the last night broke off, repeating his question from kayfa on. qāla li-, “to say to”: li- marks the one spoken to. In kayfa yakūnu hādhā jawābaka, hādhā is the subject of yakūnu and jawābaka its predicate, in the accusative. bayna, “between”, here “among, in the midst of”.

sentences.t: وَلَكِنْ أَنْتَ إِلَى الْآنَ مَا أَدَّبَكَ أَحَدٌ
sentences.tr: wa-lākin anta ilā al-āna mā addabaka aḥadun
sentences.l: But you, until the-now, not has-disciplined-you anyone.
sentences.i: But no one has taught you manners to this day.
sentences.n: Repeated from the end of the last night. wa-lākin anta: anta stands first as the topic and is picked up by -ka in addabaka. addaba, Form II, “to teach manners, discipline, chastise”; mā with the perfect negates it. The madda of الآن and the shadda of ادّبك are printed.

sentences.t: أَمَا تَعْلَمُ أَنَّ هَذَا الْأَمْرَ الَّذِي صَدَرَ مِنْكَ لَوْ صَدَرَ مِنْ عَامِّيٍّ مِنَ الْعَوَامِّ لَكَانَ ذَلِكَ قَبِيحًا مِنْهُ
sentences.tr: amā taʿlamu anna hādhā al-amra alladhī ṣadara minka law ṣadara min ʿāmmiyyin mina al-ʿawāmmi la-kāna dhālika qabīḥan minhu
sentences.l: Do-you not know that this the-matter which issued from-you, if it-had-issued from a-commoner of the-commoners, would-have-been that ugly from-him?
sentences.i: Do you not know that if what you have done had been done by some man of the common people, it would have been a disgrace even in him?”
sentences.n: amā, “do you not …?”, expects the answer yes. ṣadara min, “to issue from”, is said of a deed or a word that comes from someone: the thing he has done. hādhā al-amra is the noun of anna, and the whole law-sentence is its predicate, with dhālika taking it up again. law … la-kāna, “if … it would have been”: law sets a supposition contrary to fact, and la- opens the answer. ʿāmmī, “a commoner”, is a relative adjective from al-ʿāmma, “the common people”, and min al-ʿawāmm, “of the commoners”, presses the point: ugly even in the lowest, and how much more in a king's son. qabīḥan minhu, “ugly from him”: min marks the one in whom the deed is shameful. The print has عامي with no shadda; the doubled m and y are ours.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ إِنَّ الْمَلِكَ أَمَرَ الْمَمَالِيكَ أَنْ يَحُلُّوا كِتَافَهُ وَيَحْبِسُوهُ فِي بُرْجٍ مِنْ أَبْرَاجِ الْقَلْعَةِ
sentences.tr: thumma inna al-malika amara al-mamālīka an yaḥullū kitāfahu wa-yaḥbisūhu fī burjin min abrāji al-qalʿati
sentences.l: Then indeed the-king ordered the-mamluks that they-untie his-bonds and imprison-him in a-tower of (the) towers of the-citadel.
sentences.i: Then the king ordered the mamluks to untie his bonds and shut him up in one of the towers of the citadel.
sentences.n: kitāf is the cord that pinioned his arms behind his back at the end of the last night, when the mamluks bound him (kattafūhu). ḥalla, “to untie, loosen”, so yaḥullū kitāfahu is “untie his bonds”. amara here takes the people ordered as its object and an with the subjunctive for what they are to do: yaḥullū, yaḥbisūhu (the silent alif of -ū is dropped before the suffix). burj, “tower”, plural abrāj; min is partitive, “a tower of the towers”, that is, one of them. The shadda of يحلّوا is printed.

sentences.t: فَعِنْدَ ذَلِكَ أَخَذُوهُ وَدَخَلُوا بِهِ إِلَى بُرْجٍ عَتِيقٍ فِيهِ قَاعَةٌ خَرِبَةٌ وَفِي وَسَطِ الْقَاعَةِ بِئْرٌ خَرِبَةٌ عَتِيقَةٌ
sentences.tr: fa-ʿinda dhālika akhadhūhu wa-dakhalū bihi ilā burjin ʿatīqin fīhi qāʿatun kharibatun wa-fī wasaṭi al-qāʿati biʾrun kharibatun ʿatīqatun
sentences.l: So at that they-took-him and entered with-him to a-tower old, in-it a-hall ruined, and in (the) middle of the-hall a-well ruined, old.
sentences.i: At that they took him and brought him into an old tower, with a ruined hall in it, and in the middle of the hall an old, ruined well.
sentences.n: dakhala bi-, “to enter with”, is “to bring (someone) in”: bi- marks the one brought. fīhi qāʿatun kharibatun describes the tower, “in it a ruined hall”: after an indefinite noun Arabic needs no word for “which”. kharib, “ruined, derelict”; ʿatīq, “old”. biʾr, “well”, is feminine, so its adjectives are kharibatun ʿatīqatun; the print writes the hamza (ئ); in colloquial speech the word is often bīr. The words pile up, an old tower, a ruined hall, a ruined old well, to show a place long abandoned.

sentences.t: فَكَنَسُوهَا وَمَسَحُوا بَلَاطَهَا وَنَصَبُوا لِقَمَرِ الزَّمَانِ فِيهَا سَرِيرًا وَفَرَشُوا لَهُ عَلَى السَّرِيرِ طَرَّاحَةً وَنِطْعًا وَوَضَعُوا لَهُ مِخَدَّةً وَأَتَوْا لَهُ بِفَانُوسٍ كَبِيرٍ وَشَمْعَةٍ لِأَنَّ ذَلِكَ الْمَكَانَ كَانَ مُظْلِمًا فِى النَّهَارِ
sentences.tr: fa-kanasūhā wa-masaḥū balāṭahā wa-naṣabū li-Qamari al-Zamāni fīhā sarīran wa-farashū lahu ʿalā al-sarīri ṭarrāḥatan wa-niṭʿan wa-waḍaʿū lahu mikhaddatan wa-ataw lahu bi-fānūsin kabīrin wa-shamʿatin li-anna dhālika al-makāna kāna muẓliman fī al-nahāri
sentences.l: So they-swept-it and wiped its-paving, and set-up for-Qamar al-Zamān in-it a-bed, and spread for-him on the-bed a-mattress and a-leather-mat, and put for-him a-pillow, and came for-him with-a-lantern big and a-candle, because that the-place was dark in the-daytime.
sentences.i: They swept the hall and wiped down its paving, and set up a bed in it for Qamar al-Zamān. On the bed they spread a mattress and a leather mat for him and laid a pillow, and they brought him a large lantern and a candle, because the place was dark even by day.
sentences.n: The -hā of kanasūhā, balāṭahā and fīhā is the hall (qāʿa, feminine); balāṭ is its floor of stone flags. naṣaba, “to set up”, of a bedstead raised off the floor. ṭarrāḥa is a thick mattress or quilt laid on a bed or a divan; niṭʿ a spread of leather, the same word used elsewhere for the leather mat laid down at an execution, here only a cover for the bed. mikhadda, “pillow”, from khadd, “cheek”: what the cheek rests on. atā bi-, “to come with”, is “to bring”: bi- marks what is brought, and lahu the one it is brought for. The print writes في as فى in fī al-nahāri, as it often does. The shaddas of طرّاحة and مخدّة and the kasra of لِقمر are printed.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ إِنَّ الْمَمَالِيكَ أَدْخَلُوا قَمَرَ الزَّمَانِ فِي ذَلِكَ الْمَكَانِ وَجَعَلُوا عَلَى بَابِ الْقَاعَةِ خَادِمًا
sentences.tr: thumma inna al-mamālīka adkhalū Qamara al-Zamāni fī dhālika al-makāni wa-jaʿalū ʿalā bābi al-qāʿati khādiman
sentences.l: Then indeed the-mamluks made-enter Qamar al-Zamān into that the-place, and placed on (the) door of the-hall a-servant.
sentences.i: Then the mamluks put Qamar al-Zamān into that place and set a servant on guard at the door of the hall.
sentences.n: adkhala, Form IV of dakhala, “to make enter, put in”. jaʿala ʿalā al-bāb, “to set at the door”: the khādim placed “on” the door is its guard. In palace stories a khādim, “servant”, is often a eunuch.

sentences.t: فَعِنْدَ ذَلِكَ طَلَعَ قَمَرُ الزَّمَانِ فَوْقَ ذَلِكَ السَّرِيرِ وَهُوَ مُنْكَسِرُ الْخَاطِرِ حَزِينُ الْفُؤَادِ وَقَدْ عَاتَبَ نَفْسَهُ وَنَدِمَ عَلَى مَاجَرَى مِنْهُ فِي حَقِّ وَالِدِهِ حَيْثُ لَايَنْفَعُهُ النَّدَمُ
sentences.tr: fa-ʿinda dhālika ṭalaʿa Qamaru al-Zamāni fawqa dhālika al-sarīri wa-huwa munkasiru al-khāṭiri ḥazīnu al-fuʾādi wa-qad ʿātaba nafsahu wa-nadima ʿalā mā jarā minhu fī ḥaqqi wālidihi ḥaythu lā yanfaʿuhu al-nadamu
sentences.l: So at that, went-up Qamar al-Zamān over that the-bed, and he (was) broken of the-mind, sad of the-heart; and he-had reproached himself and regretted over what-passed from-him in (the) due of his-father, where not profits-him the-regret.
sentences.i: Then Qamar al-Zamān climbed up onto the bed, broken in spirit and sad at heart. He reproached himself and repented of the way he had behaved toward his father, now that repentance could do him no good.
sentences.n: ṭalaʿa, “to go up”, of climbing onto the raised bed. munkasiru al-khāṭiri ḥazīnu al-fuʾādi, “broken of mind, sad of heart”: each adjective is in construct with the noun it qualifies, and the two phrases are built alike; wa-huwa … is a circumstantial clause, “he being …”. ʿātaba, Form III, “to reproach”, with nafsahu, “himself”. nadima ʿalā, “to regret”: ʿalā marks what is regretted. mā jarā minhu fī ḥaqqi wālidihi, “what had passed from him with regard to his father”: jarā min is said of what someone has said or done, and fī ḥaqqi, “in the right of”, means “toward, with regard to” the person it touched. ḥaythu, properly “where”, here means “seeing that, now that”, as often in this text. The print runs mā into jarā and lā into yanfaʿuhu, as it often does.

sentences.t: وَقَالَ لَعَنَ اللَّهُ الزَّوَاجَ وَالْبَنَاتِ وَالنِّسَاءَ الْخَائِنَاتِ فَيَا لَيْتَنِي سَمِعْتُ مِنْ وَالِدِي وَتَزَوَّجْتُ فَلَوْ فَعَلْتُ ذَلِكَ كَانَ أَحْسَنَ لِي مِنْ هَذَا السِّجْنِ
sentences.tr: wa-qāla laʿana Allāhu al-zawāja wa-al-banāti wa-al-nisāʾa al-khāʾināti fa-yā laytanī samiʿtu min wālidī wa-tazawwajtu fa-law faʿaltu dhālika kāna aḥsana lī min hādhā al-sijni
sentences.l: And he-said: Cursed God the-marriage and the-girls and the-women the-treacherous! So O would-that-I had-heard from my-father and married; for if I-had-done that, it-was better for-me than this the-prison.
sentences.i: And he said, “God curse marriage, and girls, and faithless women! Oh, if only I had listened to my father and married! Had I done so, it would have been better for me than this prison.”
sentences.n: laʿana Allāhu, “God cursed”: the perfect is used as a wish, “may God curse”, as in blessings and curses generally. al-khāʾināt, “the treacherous (women)”, from khāna, “to betray”: the prince's old distrust of women, his reason for refusing to marry. yā before layta calls no one; it is a cry, “oh, would that …”. samiʿa min, “to hear from”, is “to listen to, heed”. In fa-law faʿaltu dhālika kāna aḥsana lī, the answer to law comes without la- (compare la-kāna above); both are good Arabic. aḥsana, the elative, “better”, is the predicate of kāna, and min, “than”. The ئ of الخائنات is printed.

sentences.t: هَذَا مَا كَانَ مِنْ أَمْرِ قَمَرِ الزَّمَانِ وَأَمَّا مَا كَانَ مِنْ أَمْرِ أَبِيهِ فَإِنَّهُ أَقَامَ عَلَى كُرْسِيِّ مَمْلَكَتِهِ بَقِيَّةَ الْيَوْمِ إِلَى وَقْتِ الْغُرُوبِ
sentences.tr: hādhā mā kāna min amri Qamari al-Zamāni wa-ammā mā kāna min amri abīhi fa-innahu aqāma ʿalā kursiyyi mamlakatihi baqiyyata al-yawmi ilā waqti al-ghurūbi
sentences.l: This (is) what was of (the) affair of Qamar al-Zamān. And as-for what was of (the) affair of his-father, indeed-he stayed on (the) throne of his-kingdom (the) rest of the-day until (the) time of the-sunset.
sentences.i: So much for Qamar al-Zamān. As for his father, he stayed on the throne of his kingdom for the rest of the day, until sunset.
sentences.n: hādhā mā kāna min amri …, wa-ammā mā kāna min amri …, “this is what there was of the affair of …; and as for the affair of …”, is the storyteller's formula for leaving one character and turning to another. ammā, “as for”, is answered by fa-: fa-innahu, “why, he …”. aqāma, Form IV, “to stay, remain”, and baqiyyata al-yawmi, accusative of time, “for the rest of the day”. The shadda of كرسيّ is printed.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ خَلَا بِا لْوَزِيرِ فَقَالَ لَهُ اعْلَمْ أَيُّهَا الْوَزِيرُ أَنَّكَ كُنْتَ السَّبَبَ فِي هَذَا الَّذِي جَرَى بَيْنِي وَبَيْنَ وَلَدِي كُلِّهِ حَيْثُ أَشَرْتَ عَلَيَّ بِمَا أَشَرْتَ فَمَا الَّذِي تُشِيرُ بِهِ عَلَيَّ أَنْ أَفْعَلَهُ الْآنَ
sentences.tr: thumma khalā bi-al-wazīri fa-qāla lahu iʿlam ayyuhā al-wazīru annaka kunta al-sababa fī hādhā alladhī jarā baynī wa-bayna waladī kullihi ḥaythu asharta ʿalayya bi-mā asharta fa-mā alladhī tushīru bihi ʿalayya an afʿalahu al-āna
sentences.l: Then he-was-alone with-the-vizier and said to-him: Know, O vizier, that-you were the-cause in this which happened between-me and between my-son, all-of-it, since you-advised upon-me with-what you-advised. So what (is) that-which you-advise with-it upon-me, that I-do-it now?
sentences.i: Then he withdrew alone with the vizier and said to him, “Know, O vizier, that you were the cause of all this that has happened between me and my son, since you gave me the advice you gave. So what do you advise me to do now?”
sentences.n: khalā bi-, “to be alone with”: bi- marks the companion. He is alone with the vizier, away from the court. The print sets با لوزير with a space after the alif, splitting bi-al-wazīri in two; it is read as one word. ashāra ʿalā … bi-, “to advise”: ʿalā marks the person advised and bi- the advice; bi-mā asharta, “with what you advised”, avoids repeating it, “the advice you gave”. ḥaythu again “since, seeing that”. kullihi, “all of it”, belongs to hādhā, genitive after fī, though it comes after the clause. In an afʿalahu, “that I should do it”, -hu takes up alladhī. The shadda of عليّ (twice) and the madda of الآن are printed.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ لَهُ الْوَزِيرُ أَيُّهَا الْمَلِكُ دَعْ وَلَدَكَ فِى السِّجْنِ مُدَّةَ خَمْسَةَ عَشَرَ يَوْمًا ثُمَّ أَحْضِرْهُ بَيْنَ يَدَيْكَ وَأْمُرْهُ بِالزَّوَاجِ فَإِنَّهُ لَا يُخَالِفُكَ أَبَدًا
sentences.tr: fa-qāla lahu al-wazīru ayyuhā al-maliku daʿ waladaka fī al-sijni muddata khamsata ʿashara yawman thumma aḥḍirhu bayna yadayka wa-ʾmurhu bi-al-zawāji fa-innahu lā yukhālifuka abadan
sentences.l: So said to-him the-vizier: O king, leave your-son in the-prison (a) period of five-ten day; then bring-him between your-two-hands and command-him with-the-marriage; for indeed-he will-not oppose-you ever.
sentences.i: The vizier said to him, “O king, leave your son in prison for fifteen days, then bring him before you and command him to marry. He will never go against you.”
sentences.n: daʿ, imperative of wadaʿa, “leave, let be”. muddata, “for a period of”, accusative of duration. khamsata ʿashara, “five (and) ten”, is “fifteen”: it does not change for case, and a number from eleven to ninety-nine takes its noun in the accusative singular, yawman, “day”. bayna yadayka, “between your two hands”, is “before you”. wa-ʾmurhu, “and command him”, imperative of amara after wa-, with the hamza pronounced; here the print itself writes it, أ. The verb amara chooses bi-, which marks what is commanded: bi-al-zawāji, “to marry”. lā with the imperfect and abadan, “ever”, is “never”. The print again writes في as فى.

sentences.t: وَأَدْرَكَ شَهْرَزَادَ الصَّبَاحُ فَسَكَتَتْ عَنِ الْكَلَامِ الْمُبَاحِ
sentences.tr: wa-adraka Shahrazāda al-ṣabāḥu fa-sakatat ʿani al-kalāmi al-mubāḥi
sentences.l: And the morning overtook Shahrazād, and she-fell-silent from the permitted speech.
sentences.i: And morning overtook Shahrazād, and she fell silent from the speech allowed her.
sentences.n: The object comes before the subject: Shahrazāda is the one overtaken, al-ṣabāḥu the morning. The formula rhymes al-ṣabāḥu / al-mubāḥi.
